title: Tamar (2 Samuel 13)
hook: a king's daughter is violated and silenced; the text names the wrong plainly

segments.voice: Yesterday David rose from the ground after his child died. Your line was I shall go to him. A new week begins, and today's story is a hard one.

A note before we begin: today's story is about sexual violence. It's told without detail, and if you need to stop, that's fine. Tamar is a daughter of King David, the sister of Absalom. Her half-brother Amnon becomes fixated on her. His cousin and friend Jonadab hands him a plan: pretend to be sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for you. David sends her. She kneads the dough in front of her brother and bakes the cakes. She has no reason to be afraid.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER.` → `A PLAN TO GET HER ALONE.` → `SHE COMES TO COOK.`

segments.voice: Amnon sends everyone out and takes hold of her. The first thing to notice: Tamar speaks. She says no. This is not done in Israel, she says; do not do this wanton thing. She asks where she could carry her shame, and what he would become. She even offers a way out: speak to the king; he will not keep me from you. He will not listen. He is stronger, and he forces her. Then, the text says, he hates her more than he had loved her, and has her thrown out and the door bolted. Tamar doesn't go quietly. She tears the long robe the king's unmarried daughters wore, puts ashes on her head, lays her hand on it, and goes away crying aloud. The second thing to notice: the Bible names this as a wrong. It doesn't blur it or blame her. It gives her words, and records her grief in public. Then the silencing. Absalom says: hold your peace, my sister; he is your brother; don't take this to heart. And Tamar "remained desolate" in her brother Absalom's house. King David hears all of it and is very angry. The text doesn't say he does anything. Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, and waits. Much of what follows grows out of that silence: a murder, a rebellion, a war between father and son. Why is this chapter here? In a palace where the powerful wanted it quiet, the text remembers her name, her words, and her torn robe. Her story is told.
screen: `TAMAR SAYS NO.` · `HE FORCES HER, THEN HATES HER.` · `SHE TEARS HER ROBE AND CRIES ALOUD.` · then: `HOLD YOUR PEACE, MY SISTER.` · then, large: `HER STORY IS TOLD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who might one day bring you something painful, and picture yourself listening without what Absalom said: not hush, not don't take it to heart, just I believe you, and I'm here. If this story touched your own life, simply breathe, and know that yours deserves to be told too. If you pray, you can remember Tamar and everyone like her.
Tamar. A king's daughter who said no, was wronged, and was told to be quiet, and whose story the text refused to drop. Today's word.
Your line: her story is told. The text refused to let it be hushed. Until tomorrow, gently.

howItsDone: Jews read the story of Tamar as part of the book of Samuel; some teachers today use it to talk openly about sexual violence and about believing those who come forward.

chat.says: Why would the Bible include such a painful story about Tamar?
options: To name the wrong, give Tamar her own words, and remember her grief.
To show Absalom handled it well by keeping everything quiet.
To show King David punished Amnon at once for what he did.
chat.meaning: The text gives Tamar words, records her torn robe and her cries, and names the wrong, though the palace told her to hold her peace.
